state.misconception_label: Assumes that an arrow on a number line starts at zero

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: ![Number line with -12 and -7 marked. Starting at -12, follow an arrow pointing to the right labelled +10. Then there is an arrow labelled b pointing to the left, which ends at -7 on the number line.]() What is the value of \( b \) ? I got \( -7 \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you were moving along a number line with everyday objects like toys or books. If you start at -12 and move to the right by +10, then move back to the left by an unknown amount, where would you end up?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, so if I start at -12 and move to the right by +10, I think I would end up at -2. But then if I move back to the left, I’m not sure how to figure out how much I need to move back to get to -7. Can you help me understand that part better?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you were playing a game where you start at -12 and move to the right by +10, landing at -2. Now, think about moving back to the left to reach -7. What would be the value of the arrow pointing to the left that gets you to -7?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, so if I start at -2 and I want to get to -7, I guess I need to move back to the left. But how do I figure out how much that is? Is it just like counting the spaces on the number line?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher never directly addresses the misconception that arrows start at zero, instead repeatedly asking the student to imagine the scenario without providing the conceptual clarity needed; while the student does correctly calculate -12 + 10 = -2 by Turn 2, they remain uncertain about how to find the value of b even by Turn 4.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher attempts to use concrete analogies (toys, books, playing a game) to ground the number line problem, but these references remain superficial and don't deeply connect the abstract mathematical operations to meaningful real-world experiences that would help the student understand the concept.
